accuracy.evidence: Checked against the EEF Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance (2018) plan, monitor, evaluate cycle, CCSS Mathematical Practice 1 (monitor and evaluate progress and change course if necessary, try simpler forms of the problem) and the England National Curriculum maths aims on breaking problems into simpler steps and persevering. Every worked sum is correct: 23 stars as four fives and three, 3 floors of 4 windows is 12, and 12 add 9 as 12 add 10 take 1 is 21.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the belief that trying harder at the same method is the same as persevering (the same again prediction and the fourth-time challenge option), the perseveration slip of repeating a failed count (Ben counting one by one again is refused with feedback), and the opposite slip of abandoning a method that already works (the work this time card must go to same again, and give up is answered with a gentle redirect).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagswap is built around switching strategy after a failed try: a robot that bumps a wall and must reroute, a star field that only becomes countable when grouped into fives, a same again or new approach sort, matching problems to draw it, break it into parts or work backwards, and judging which of two worked tries succeeded. flagtry is about persisting with practice and flagthink about planning first; it passed the 30 percent shingle gate against every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child watches a one by one count of the stars go wrong, then taps the stars into groups of five and gets 23 at once, so the payoff of changing method is felt rather than told. The robot only reaches the flag after a different route, and the judge step puts a lost count next to a tidy add ten take one, so the child compares two strategies on the same sum.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong answers: whether pushing the robot into the wall again will work, whether counting the stars one by one again will fix Ben's lost count, and whether doing a sum the same way always gives the same result. Each step then shows the outcome (the robot bumps again, grouping beats recounting, the same method gives the same answer) and the done message echoes the child's choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge asks what to do when a sum is still wrong after three tries the same way, with try a new way, do it the same way a fourth time and give up as options. Every wrong tap gets its own message (the same way gives the same result; stopping means the sum never gets solved) and every lab step has at least three specific feedback lines, such as wall bumps naming a new direction.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs measure about grade 0.1 and adult paragraphs about grade 7.7 by the Flesch-Kincaid gate, under the family targets of 5.0 and 10.0. Kid sentences are short and concrete (Ben got 22, then 24), and adult text explains cognitive flexibility, metacognition and perseveration in plain words with one classroom example each.

no_filler.evidence: No stock filler phrases; every paragraph adds a fact, an example or a step to try. The adult section gives a concrete script (what did you try, what happened, what else could you try) and names the common mistake of praising effort on a method that is clearly not working instead of prompting a switch.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough on iPhone 13 and desktop completed every Show me demo with a tick inside 6 seconds, including the custom star grouping schedule that waits for the 900 ms tween. Screenshots in dark and light themes show the maze, star field, sort bins and strategy cards fitting the phone width, with large young-mode buttons for arrows, groups and choices.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reported no violations in light or dark themes on desktop and iPhone, and there were no console errors. Every lab button has an explicit aria-label naming its action (move up, put the stars in groups of 5, same again), the canvas has an aria-label, step results are announced through the say helper, and motion falls back when reduced motion is set.

DfE (2013) National Curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, aims (problem solving, breaking problems into simpler steps, persevering) and Year 2 addition and subtraction
